rows.l: - For Sheet-Level Manipulation questions, modify or fill in values ONLY within the cell range given in answer_position — never touch cells outside that range.
- Prefer computing and writing LITERAL values (e.g. with pandas/openpyxl) over live spreadsheet formulas, so the result is unambiguous when the file is re-opened for grading.

+- The graded artifact is the resulting DATA, never source code. If the instruction asks for a "macro", "VBA", "VB code", a "script", or "code" that performs an operation, do NOT write that code text into any cell — perform the operation yourself in Python and write only its resulting values. (A cell containing the text `Sub DeleteRows()` is always wrong; the deleted/shifted data is the answer.)

+- When you read source cells to compute a sum, lookup, or other aggregate, read their COMPUTED values — load with `openpyxl(..., data_only=True)` or `pandas.read_excel`. A plain `openpyxl` read returns a formula cell as its formula STRING (e.g. `'=SUM(A7:G7)'`), which numeric conversion silently skips, so any total that includes a formula cell comes out too low. If a computed value comes back `None` (a cached result missing on some copies), derive it from its own inputs before using it — never let a missing value act as 0.

+- Compute every answer from values you read out of the CURRENT file at run time; never hardcode a number, cell address, or row/column count you saw only in the preview. Within answer_position, change ONLY the cells the instruction actually asks you to change — leave any cell the instruction says is already correct, or does not mention, at its original value; do not overwrite a cell just because it falls inside the range.

+- When you copy or shift existing cell values, preserve them in their native form — do not convert or stringify them (e.g. avoid round-tripping through a `dtype=object` DataFrame, which can turn numbers into text). Copy text as text (including date-like text such as `'2022/09/08'`, which stays text), and leave numbers and real dates in whatever form the source already stores them. Do NOT convert text to dates or apply rounding the instruction did not request.
- Always save your result to the exact output_path given, creating any missing parent directories first.
- If code execution returns an error, read the traceback carefully and fix the code — do not repeat a failing approach unchanged.

+### if the instruction anchors row-deletion on a marker text
+This applies ONLY when the instruction tells you to delete rows located relative to a
+specific marker text/label found in a column (e.g. "delete the blank rows above each
+'<HEADER>'"). If instead it just says to remove all blank rows with no such marker, delete
+ONLY the genuinely blank rows and skip this section.
+- The region to remove is the whole separator between two data sections, not just the
+  literally-blank rows. Between sections that separator often ALSO contains non-data rows:
+  a section-label row, and a repeated column-header row. Delete the entire block.
+- When the instruction gives an example row range (e.g. "delete rows 29 to 36"), inspect
+  exactly those rows and make your rule reproduce that range precisely — note whether the
+  marker row itself falls inside the range and must be deleted too.
+- Find each block's extent DYNAMICALLY: from the marker, walk toward the previous section
+  and keep removing rows until you reach a genuine data row (a row carrying real record
+  values), then stop. Do not stop at the first non-blank row — label/header rows are
+  non-blank yet still part of the separator. Apply the same rule to EVERY marker occurrence.
+- Delete/shift rows with openpyxl so surviving cells keep their original types; avoid
+  rebuilding the sheet from a `dtype=object` DataFrame, which can turn numbers into text.
+  Pack survivors to the top, leave trailing rows genuinely empty (never pad with spaces),
+  and leave every cell the instruction does not touch exactly as its original input.
